source_text: Quid si praeter pudorem, quem potiorem putant, etiam incommoda corporis reformident, quod inlotos, quod sordulentos, quod extra laetitiam oportet deversari in asperitudine sacci et horrore cineris et oris de ieiunio vanitate? Num ergo in coccino et Tyrio pro delictis supplicare nos condecet? Cedo acum crinibus distinguendis et pulverem dentibus elimandis et bisulcum aliquid ferri vel aeris unguibus repastinandis, si quid ficti nitoris, si quid coacti ruboris in labia aut genas urgeat. Praeterea exquirito balneas laetiores hortulani maritimive secessus, adiicito ad sumptum, conquirito altilium enormem saginam, defaecato senectutem vini, cumque quis interrogarit, cuinam ea largiaris, Deliqui, dicito, in deum, et periclitor in aeternum perire; itaque nunc pendeo et maceror et excrucior, ut deum reconciliem mihi, quem delinquendo laesi. Sed enim illos, qui ambitu obeunt capessendi magistratus, neque pudet neque piget incommodis animae et corporis, nec incommodis tantum, verum et contumeliis omnibus eniti in causa votorum suorum. Quas non ignobilitates vestium affectant? quae non atria nocturnis et crudis salutationibus occupant? ad omnem occursum maioris cuiusque personae decrescentes, nullis conviviis celebres, nullis comessationibus congreges, sed exules a libertatis et laetitiae felicitate, idque totum propter unius anni volaticum gaudium. Nos, quod securium virgarumve petitio sustinet, in periculo aeternitatis tolerare dubitamus? et castigationem victus atque cultus offenso domino praestare cessabimus, quae gentiles nemine omnino laeso sibi irrogant? Hi sunt de quibus scriptura commemorat: Vae illis qui delicta sua velut procero fune nectunt.
thought_title: The absurdity of luxury while seeking reconciliation
orientation: Tertullian is addressing those who shrink from the public confession because of its bodily discomforts, and he now contrasts their pampering of the body with the self-denial that even pagans undergo for worldly ambition.
pass_a_gloss: What if, beyond the shame, which they consider the greater thing, they also dread the bodily discomforts, because unwashed, because filthy, because outside of joy one must lodge in the roughness of sackcloth and the griminess of ashes and the emptiness of the face from fasting? Are we then suited to plead for our sins in scarlet and Tyrian purple? Give me a needle for arranging the hair and powder for polishing the teeth and some two-pronged tool of iron or bronze for digging around the nails, if anything of artificial shine, if anything of forced redness presses upon the lips or cheeks. Furthermore, seek out the more pleasant baths of a garden or a seaside retreat, add to the expense, hunt down the enormous fattening of a fatted bird, clarify the old age of wine, and when someone asks, for whom you lavish these things, say: I have sinned against God, and I am in danger of perishing forever; therefore now I hang and am worn down and am tortured, so that I may reconcile God to myself, whom I have offended by sinning. But indeed those who go about with canvassing for obtaining magistracies are neither ashamed nor reluctant to strive with discomforts of soul and body, and not only with discomforts, but also with all insults, in the cause of their desires. What ignobilities of clothing do they not affect? What halls do they not occupy with nocturnal and undigested greetings? diminishing themselves at every encounter with each greater person, celebrated at no banquets, gathered at no revelries, but exiles from the happiness of freedom and joy, and all that for the sake of the fleeting joy of one year. Do we hesitate to endure, in the danger of eternity, what the pursuit of axes or rods sustains? And shall we cease to offer to the offended Lord the chastisement of food and dress, which the gentiles impose upon themselves with no one at all offended? These are they of whom the scripture records: Woe to those who tie their sins together like a long rope.

choices.term: in asperitudine sacci et horrore cineris
choices.english: in the roughness of sackcloth and the griminess of ashes
choices.why: Keeps the physical, unpleasant texture of the penitential materials, matching the literal force of asperitudo and horror.
rejected: in rough sackcloth and horrible ashes
in the harshness of sackcloth and the horror of ashes

choices.english: the emptiness of the face from fasting
choices.why: Vanitas here means the hollow, wasted look produced by fasting; 'emptiness' preserves the literal sense.
rejected: the vanity of the face from fasting
the hollowness of the face from fasting

choices.english: I have sinned against God, say
choices.why: Delinquo in deum means to sin against God; the imperative dicito is kept as a command.
rejected: Say: I have sinned against God

choices.english: I hang and am worn down and am tortured
choices.why: Pendeo is literal 'I hang' (in suspense or torment), and the three verbs are kept in their physical, present-tense force.
rejected: I am in suspense and am wasted and am tormented
I am hanging and wasting away and being tortured

choices.english: the pursuit of axes or rods
choices.why: Secures and virgae are the symbols of Roman magistrates' power; the literal objects are kept to show what candidates seek.
rejected: the canvassing for axes or rods

choices.term: delicta sua velut procero fune nectunt
choices.english: tie their sins together like a long rope
choices.why: The image is of sins being knotted or bound together into a long rope; 'tie together' preserves the verb necto.
rejected: bind their sins like a long rope
weave their sins as with a long rope

bible_refs.note: Vae illis qui delicta sua velut procero fune nectunt

pass_b_english: What if, beyond the modesty they consider so important, they also dread the bodily discomforts—having to stay unwashed, filthy, outside all festivity, in the roughness of sackcloth and the griminess of ashes, with the emptiness of the face from fasting? Are we then to plead for our sins dressed in scarlet and Tyrian purple? Hand me the pin for parting the hair and the powder for polishing the teeth and some two-pronged tool of iron or bronze for scraping the nails. Apply whatever artificial shine, whatever forced redness, to lips or cheeks. What is more, seek out the more pleasant baths in gardens or seaside retreats, add to the expense, hunt down enormous fattened fowl, clarify the aged wine—and when someone asks you for whom you are lavishing all this, say: I have sinned against God, and I am in danger of perishing forever. So now I hang and am worn down and am tortured, so that I may reconcile God to me, whom I injured by sinning.

But those who go about canvassing for public office are neither ashamed nor reluctant to strive with every disadvantage of soul and body—and not only disadvantages, but every kind of insult—for the sake of what they desire. What shabby clothing do they not put on? What doorways do they not occupy with nighttime and undigested greetings? They shrink at every encounter with any person of greater rank, celebrated at no banquets, gathered at no feasts, but exiled from the happiness of freedom and festivity—and all of it for the fleeting joy of a single year. We, though the desire for secure rods sustains us, doubt whether we can endure the danger of eternity? And shall we refuse to offer to an offended Lord the discipline of food and dress that the nations impose on themselves when no one at all has been injured? These are the ones of whom Scripture says: Woe to those who tie their sins together like a long rope (Jeremiah 9:4).

problems.quote: when what the pursuit of axes or rods endures is at stake, hesitate to endure it in the danger of eternity?
problems.source_quote: Nos, quod securum virgarumve petitio sustinet, in periculo aeternitatis tolerare dubitamus?
problems.why: The English rendering is garbled and does not convey the Latin sense of “though the desire for secure rods sustains us, we doubt whether we can endure the danger of eternity.”
problems.fix: We, though the desire for secure rods sustains us, doubt whether we can endure the danger of eternity.

problems.why: 'Repastinare' means scraping/cleaning, not trenching; agricultural metaphor misread.
Latin 'mihi' is dative of reference (for myself/to my advantage), not 'to myself' as object; God is reconciled to the sinner, not vice versa.
problems.ruling: reconciliem mihi = reconcile God to me, not to myself

problems.source_quote: Vae illis qui delicta sua velut procero fune nectunt.
problems.why: The cited verse does not match the Latin quotation; the correct reference is Jeremiah 9:4 (LXX).
problems.ruling: Latin quotes Isaiah 5:18 (Vulgate: 'Vae qui trahunt iniquitatem in funiculis vanitatis'), not Jeremiah 9:4.

edits.new: though the desire for secure rods sustains us, doubt whether we can endure the danger of eternity?

fixed: The English rendering of 'Nos, quod securum virgarumve petitio sustinet, in periculo aeternitatis tolerare dubitamus?' was garbled; corrected to convey the Latin sense.
'Repastinare' means scraping/cleaning, not trenching; corrected to 'scraping the nails'.
Latin 'mihi' is dative of reference; corrected to 'reconcile God to me'.
The Latin quotation 'Vae illis qui delicta sua velut procero fune nectunt' corresponds to Jeremiah 9:4 (LXX), not Isaiah 5:18; corrected the citation.

last_rejected.source_quote: Vae illis qui delicta sua velut procero fune nectunt
last_rejected.why: The citation Jeremiah 9:4 does not match this quotation. The verse about tying sins with a long rope is Isaiah 5:18 (LXX/Vulgate tradition).
last_rejected.ruling: Phrase matches Vulgate Jeremiah 9:4; citation is correct.

last_rejected.quote: I have sinned against God, and I am in danger of perishing forever.
last_rejected.source_quote: Deliqui, dicito, in deum, et periclitor in aeternum perire
last_rejected.why: Latin does not say “I have sinned against God”; it says “Deliqui… in deum”, which does not contain that confession.
last_rejected.fix: …say, “I have left to God, and I am in danger of perishing forever.”
last_rejected.ruling: Deliqui in deum = 'I have offended against God'; 'sinned' is within normal semantic range of delinquo.
